column4: The hypocrites stand for prayer lazily, seek human notice in يراؤون الناس, and remember God only a little; it gathers absent-hearted prayer and the refusal to be overlooked into one scene.

The command ولا تعد عيناك عنهم forbids the eye to pass beyond inconspicuous worshippers toward worldly adornment, while أغفلنا قلبه names the heedless heart; this directly stages the section's gaze and heart.
فأنت عنه تلهى makes distraction from the earnest blind visitor the climax of 80:1-9, a concrete case of attention passing over the less socially dazzling person.
كلا بل لا تكرمون اليتيم names failure to honor the orphan, making the neglect carried in the section's dictionary account of يتيم explicit conduct.
Nor urging one another to feed the needy continues 89:17's neglected-orphan scene and closely matches the section's noticed absence of concern for طعام المسكين.
God's finding the Prophet an orphan and giving shelter reverses the child being left outside human attention: the orphan is found and held in view by God.
فلا تقهر turns God's sheltering of the orphan in 93:6 into a direct command against overpowering him, the clearest reversal of يدع اليتيم.
The exact form الذين هم في غمرة ساهون places the سهو root inside an engulfing غمرة, giving the section's absent heart a surrounding medium that covers it.
The hypocrites close their hands, forget God, and are consequently forgotten; bodily withholding and reciprocal neglect expose what the section's heedlessness looks like from outside.
Charity done رئاء الناس joins aid to the needful with the desire to be seen, and its denial of God and the Last Day recalls how the whole surah roots both failures in denial of judgment.
Spending only to be seen by people makes public brightness itself corrupt the act that should have reached another, precisely the section's reversal of attention.
The people of the Fire say they were not among those who prayed; with 74:44 it pairs failed prayer with failed care for the poor, the same moral adjacency as the section.
“We did not feed the needy” completes 74:43's confession about prayer, directly bringing the missing poor person's food beside empty or absent worship.
ولا يحض على طعام المسكين is the same concrete failure to urge feeding found in the surah; 69:33 supplies its setting in refusal to believe in God.
Failure to believe in God is immediately expressed in 69:34 as failure to urge feeding the needy, giving the neglect its inward source just as 107 links denial, prayer, and the orphan.
Feeding food despite loving it to a needy person, an orphan, and a captive makes the overlooked person's due visible and enacted.
The feeders of 76:8 seek no repayment or thanks, so their care is governed by God's face rather than the human gaze sought by those who show off.
The well-provided are told not to withhold from needy kin and also to pardon and overlook; it unites giving with the section's “good” kind of overlooking another's lapse.
The restrained poor are mistakenly thought rich and must be recognized by their mark; this directly explains how a needy person can disappear under an untrained gaze.
A treasure is preserved for two orphan boys until maturity because their father was righteous; divine care carries delayed good to children whose father can no longer guard it.
Orphans are tested until maturity, their property then handed over, and guardians forbidden to consume it hastily; it distinguishes protective delay from the section's negligent delay of goodness.

Orphan women are denied what is prescribed for them while others desire to marry them, and the command is to stand for orphans in justice; desire here makes the vulnerable person's right disappear from view.
Reform of orphans' affairs is declared best and mixing with them is framed as living with brothers, replacing detached neglect with sustained attention.
The refusal “Should we feed one whom God could feed?” gives speech to the exact evasion by which the poor person's food is left out.
Trade and sale do not distract these people from remembrance, prayer, or almsgiving; it directly reverses the departed heart and joins attended prayer to open-handed care.
When people see trade or amusement they scatter toward it and leave the Messenger standing, literally staging the eye's attraction to the bright diversion as worship is abandoned.
أقم الصلاة لذكري defines prayer as remembrance of God, the direct inward opposite of a heart gone away from its prayer.
Successors who أضاعوا الصلاة and follow desires embody negligence directed at prayer itself, rather than a mere accidental lapse within it.
The intoxicated may not approach prayer until they know what they are saying; awareness of one's words marks a concrete boundary against absent-minded worship.
The reminder benefits one who has a heart, gives ear, and is حاضر as a witness; these are the precise faculties missing when the heart has gone from what stands before it.
Believers are humble and inwardly present in their prayer, supplying the positive posture opposed to ساهون عن صلاتهم.
True believers' hearts tremble when God is mentioned and their faith increases on hearing His signs; 8:3 then carries this living heart into prayer and giving.
Those inwardly moved in 8:2 establish prayer and spend from God's provision, reversing both the empty prayer and withheld aid of the section.
Humble hearts at God's mention, steadfastness, established prayer, and spending are held together, showing the heart, worship, and care as one response.
Constancy in prayer, introduced by 70:22, directly opposes neglect of prayer and leads in 70:24-25 to acknowledging the poor person's share.
A recognized right in their wealth prepares 70:25's named recipients, making aid a due that cannot simply vanish from attention.
The recognized right belongs to the asker and the deprived; beside constant prayer in 70:23, it reverses the section's pairing of negligent worship and missing provision.
Those who carefully guard their prayers are the direct opposite of people whose hearts have gone away from theirs.
Righteousness is located beyond outward orientation in giving loved wealth to orphans and the needy, establishing prayer, and fulfilling commitments; it joins all the section's separated duties.
Kindness to orphans and the needy is commanded beside worship of God, while proud self-display is rejected at the verse's end.
Stinginess, urging others to stinginess, and hiding God's bounty expose the closed hand beside 4:36's orphan and needy and 4:38's ostentatious spender.
Spending in ease and hardship is joined to restraining anger and pardoning people, so aid and the section's right kind of overlooking another's fault meet in one character.
The Messenger must not drive away inconspicuous people who call on their Lord morning and evening seeking His face; sincere worshippers must remain visible despite elite pressure.
Noah's chiefs dismiss his followers as the lowest people at first glance, a direct account of sight converting low social brightness into false lack of worth.
Noah refuses to drive away the believers and grounds their worth in meeting their Lord, reversing the hand that pushes the socially disregarded person aside.
The chiefs object that the lowest people follow Noah, making social rank the brightness by which they decide whom to notice.
Noah says he will not drive away the believers, directly reversing the section's shove against the vulnerable and the elite wish to erase the lowly.
The frown opens the incident completed in 80:10: attention registers the less prestigious visitor as an interruption before his hidden worth is disclosed.
The blind man is the one who came, making the episode's overlooked figure someone whose lack of sight sharpens the moral failure of others' sight.
The overlooked visitor may purify himself; the verse exposes value invisible to the surface judgment dramatized in 80:1-2.
The self-sufficient man is the socially bright pole of the scene, receiving attention that 80:10 says was withheld from the striving visitor.
Directing one's attention to the self-sufficient person concretely stages the gaze going where prestige already shines.
The other man comes striving, giving the person passed over in 80:10 an active sincerity that outward status had concealed.
His reverent fear supplies the hidden inward brightness missed by the social gaze in the surrounding scene.
The Prophet is told not to extend his eyes toward worldly enjoyments and instead to lower his wing to believers, joining disciplined sight to gentle care for those easily passed over.
The eye must not stretch toward the flower of worldly life given to others; God's provision is declared better and more lasting, correcting the gaze that equates brightness with value.

The hypocrites' bodies impress the eye and their speech draws the ear, yet they are like propped timber; it is a precise portrait of shining enough to avoid being overlooked while inward life is absent.
Qarun goes out in his adornment and spectators desire his visible fortune, a full scene of brightness capturing the eye and defining worth.
Even a mustard-seed weight hidden in a rock, heaven, or earth is brought forth by God; what is tiny and concealed never escapes divine attention.
The boastful spender asks in effect whether anyone has seen him; God's challenge punctures concern with human visibility by asserting an inescapable witness.
In the context of a man obstructing a servant's prayer, “Does he not know that God sees?” places divine sight over both prayer and performative human power.
The one who forgot God's signs is himself left forgotten and blind, completing 20:124-25's movement from turning away to loss of sight.
Those who forget God are made to forget themselves; negligence of the highest object hollows out the negligent person, as the section's prayer loses its own heart.
Do not rebuke the petitioner extends 93:9's care from the orphan to another person easily pushed away, and answers the missing food and closed hand in the section.
“Your Lord has not forsaken you” frames the orphan recollection of 93:6: apparent delay and dimness do not mean abandonment by God.
The promise that the Lord will give until the addressee is satisfied answers the section's dictionary sense of good arriving late to the orphan.
Joseph's brothers resent that he is more present in their father's love, exposing the competition not to be overlooked that precedes their removal of another child.
They propose killing or expelling Joseph so their father's face will be exclusively theirs; this is the section's dynamic of seeking the gaze by making another disappear.
Casting the child into the hidden bottom of a well turns jealous competition for attention into a physical act of removal, as 12:9 proposed.
Jacob fears the wolf may take Joseph while the brothers are heedless of him, a direct child-and-guardian scene in which lapse of attention becomes danger.
Giving orphans their property and forbidding substitution or absorption of it prevents the guardian's appetite from making the child's right disappear.
Those who consume orphan property are said to consume fire into their bellies, revealing the grave reality hidden behind an easy act of appropriation.
The orphan's property may be approached only in the best manner until maturity, requiring sustained guardianship through the very interval named in the section's definition.
Protection of orphan property until maturity keeps the fatherless child's future continuously before the guardian rather than letting good arrive too late.
Feeding on a day of hunger is the concrete act that 90:15-16 directs toward an orphan and a person in misery.
An orphan of near kin is named as the recipient of the difficult ascent introduced by feeding in 90:14, making the solitary child a claim on action.
The needy person in dust completes the feeding scene of 90:14 and makes visible the low condition that the comfortable gaze can pass over.
A recognized share in the God-conscious person's wealth belongs to the asker and deprived, filling the section's conspicuous blank where the poor person's food should be.
Giving kin, the needy, and the traveler their due names provision as an owed right, not a favor that may be postponed until the vulnerable person is noticed.
Giving the needy and traveler their due is declared best for those seeking God's face, joining care to the right audience rather than public display.
A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by hurt, joining care with the right kind of overlooking and rejecting aid that becomes another shove.
Those who spend seeking God's pleasure and from inner certainty are the inward opposite of 2:264's performer; the fruitful garden also contrasts with the performer's bare rock.
The most mindful person gives wealth to purify himself, turning resources toward another rather than using another person as a mirror for reputation.
No favor is being repaid in the giver's act, excluding the social transaction and applause that could govern visible generosity.
Seeking only the face of the Most High supplies the direct alternative audience to showing off before people.
The hypocrites explicitly tell others not to spend on the people around the Messenger so that they disperse, weaponizing withheld provision to make the lowly disappear.
People forbidden to ridicule others are reminded that those who look lesser may be better; visible rank is therefore an unreliable measure of worth.
God knows the furtive glance and what breasts conceal, holding both the wandering eye and the absent or performative heart within divine sight.

The lamp whose glass is like a brilliantly shining star is a deliberate celestial reversal of the section's nearly missed Suha; 24:36-37 then locates that light in remembrance and undistracted prayer.
النجم الثاقب is the piercingly visible star, the opposite pole to the section's tiny hidden Suha and therefore a check on treating visibility as worth.
The comparison to protected, hidden pearls gives Quranic dignity to value not exposed to the casual gaze, reversing the assumption that what remains unseen lacks brilliance.
وما كان ربك نسيا states that the Lord is never forgetful, distinguishing divine delay from the human neglect through which the orphan is named.
Moses says his Lord neither errs nor forgets, setting divine knowledge against both the eye that misses the small and the heart that leaves its prayer.
Being forgotten on the Day because one forgot its meeting makes neglect reciprocal, as in 9:67, and reveals the final consequence of wanting human notice while ignoring God.
“Taste, because you forgot the meeting of this day; We have forgotten you” turns chosen inattention into the very exclusion the negligent person failed to fear.
Those distracted by worldly life and treating religion as play are forgotten as they forgot the meeting of the Day, linking attractive distraction to reciprocal abandonment.
“Remember Me; I will remember you” is the positive reciprocity opposite both 9:67's forgetting and the desire to secure remembrance from human spectators.
The Helpers prefer others over themselves despite their own need, reversing the self-centering gaze and closed hand that let the orphan and poor person vanish.
The command not to present oneself as pure because God best knows the mindful undercuts the performer's attempt to control how others see him.
Concealed charity to the poor is called better, marking a precise boundary between an act hidden from human eyes and one done for their eyes.
Prayer is said to restrain indecency and wrongdoing and God's remembrance is greater; its moral work exposes the emptiness of a prayer abandoned by its heart.
Careful preservation of prayers directly reverses treating them as something the heart can leave unattended.
Guarding all prayers and standing devoutly before God gives a concise positive command against negligence about prayer.
The call for believers' hearts to become humble at God's remembrance confronts the hardened or departed heart rather than merely correcting an outward posture.
Remembering the Lord's name and praying form one action, while 87:16 names preference for nearer worldly life as the competing attraction.
At the call to Friday prayer believers must leave trade; 62:11 shows the exact failure when visible commerce draws them away.
Wealth and children are the adornment of worldly life, while lasting good deeds are better with God; this corrects the eye that follows what shines now.
Worldly life is described as amusement, adornment, boasting, and rivalry in wealth before its vegetation withers, exposing why bright display is a poor guide to lasting value.
People given knowledge answer the spectators of 28:79 that God's reward is better, explicitly correcting desire awakened by Qarun's adornment.
Qarun and his house are swallowed after the display of 28:79, making the object that monopolized attention disappear beneath the earth.
The previous day's admirers recognize that worldly expansion is no proof of divine favor, revising the gaze that Qarun's glitter had captured.
The curse on the conjecturers identifies who the ساهون of 51:11 are; its own contribution is to connect engulfing heedlessness with confident speech unsupported by knowledge.
The possibility that reminder may benefit the blind visitor continues 80:3 and shows what is lost when attention passes him over.
The addressee is not accountable if the self-sufficient man refuses purification, removing the excuse for privileging him over the striving visitor of 80:8-10.
The elite ask whether these lowly believers are really those God favored, exposing the status-based misreading that motivates the forbidden expulsion in 6:52.
Noah asks who could protect him from God if he drove the believers away, giving divine weight to his refusal in 11:29 to erase the lowly from the gathering.
Noah places his followers' account with his Lord, refusing the elite demand to judge their worth by the visible social measure raised in 26:111.
The covenant places kindness to orphans and the needy beside prayer and almsgiving, an early formulation of the duties the section shows splitting apart.
When asked what to spend, the answer names orphans and the needy, making the easily delayed recipient part of the question's immediate field.
Fear of failing justice toward orphan girls changes what marriage choices are permitted, so the orphan's otherwise weak position governs the stronger person's conduct.
If orphans and needy people are present at an estate division, they must receive provision and kind speech; physical presence must lead to notice rather than exclusion.
The divine allocation of spoils assigns a share to orphans and the needy, formally preventing their claims from depending on whether powerful people happen to notice them.
Orphans and the needy receive a share so wealth does not circulate only among the rich, directly countering a social gaze and flow captured by the already prominent.
The later state being better than the first gives temporal shape to 93:3-6: a wait can hold promised good without meaning that the orphaned servant was forgotten.
God finds the Prophet in need and enriches him, continuing 93:6's repeated divine finding and supplying the provision that human neglect delays.
Speaking of the Lord's favor follows commands about the orphan and petitioner; it distinguishes grateful testimony centered on the giver from display centered on oneself.
Spending followed by neither reminder nor injury preserves the recipient's dignity and keeps generosity from becoming a public claim on another person.
Spending night and day, secretly and openly, makes consistency rather than visibility the measure of care.
Prayer and spending secretly and openly are commanded together before the day when social exchange cannot repair neglect.
Reciting God's book, establishing prayer, and spending secretly and openly describe worship whose inward remembrance issues in care.
The hand must be neither chained to the neck nor opened without limit; the chained-hand image explains the embodied stinginess named in 9:67.
The garden owners tell one another that no poor person may enter, turning the needy person's disappearance into an explicit plan.
They set out with confident power to withhold, enacting the exclusion voiced in 68:24 before the garden's loss exposes it.
The Prophet is told to pardon the companions, seek forgiveness for them, and continue consulting them, a concrete Quranic form of overlooking another's lapse well.
Those who avoid major sins forgive when angry, identifying the fault of another as a proper object of deliberate overlooking.
After allowing one party to waive a marital due, “do not forget graciousness between you” separates merciful relinquishment from forgetting another person's good.
Accepting what is easy, commanding right, and turning away from the ignorant supplies a disciplined form of passing over offense rather than passing over need.
Turning away from God's remembrance begins the sequence that ends in 20:126 with blindness and being forgotten, giving the section's departed heart a trajectory.
The resurrected person asks why he has been raised blind though he once saw, making failed spiritual attention visible before 20:126 explains it as forgetting the signs.
Hearts that do not understand, eyes that do not see, and ears that do not hear converge in the designation الغافلون, closely matching the section's joined failures of eye and heart.
Quiet, humble remembrance morning and evening ends with the command not to be among the heedless, setting sustained inward attention against سهو.
Hearts find rest in God's remembrance, presenting remembrance as the heart's settled presence rather than its departure from prayer.
Woe to hearts hardened against God's remembrance defines the inward failure behind worship that remains only an exterior act.
The question whether people reflect on the Quran or have locks on their hearts gives a bodily image for attention that cannot enter.
Wealth and children must not distract believers from God's remembrance; the verse names the attractive objects that can draw the heart away.
Rivalry for abundance distracts people until the graves, a compact account of attention captured by what is socially bright and countable.
Worldly life is beautified for disbelievers and they mock believers, showing visible attraction converting into contempt for those whose worth is less worldly.
The hypocrites come to prayer lazily and spend unwillingly, another direct joining of depleted worship with reluctant aid.
The one who is stingy and considers himself self-sufficient combines the closed hand with the status posture that receives attention in the Abasa scene.
Human transgression begins when a person sees himself as self-sufficient in 96:7, the same self-magnifying stance that pushes prayer and weaker people from view.
Seeing oneself as self-sufficient supplies the false visual judgment behind the transgression named in 96:6 and the obstruction of prayer later in the passage.
Not even an atom's weight, smaller or greater, escapes the Lord while people act; divine attention thus includes what human scale calls too small to see.
God knows the falling leaf and the grain in the earth's darkness, giving the section's hidden small object a witness who never passes over it.
The record leaves neither small nor great uncounted, reversing the human habit of letting the inconspicuous thing disappear.
The oath by celestial bodies that withdraw begins a Quranic sky scene in which apparent disappearance, completed by their movement in 81:16, remains divinely marked.
The moving bodies that hide continue 81:15's oath, offering a celestial analogue to the section's small star slipping from ordinary sight.
The infant Moses is sent onto the river yet formed “under My eye”; separation from parental sight is met by God's unbroken guardianship.
Moses is returned to his mother so her eye may be comforted, making restored human watchfulness part of the divine care announced in 20:39.
Moses' sister follows him and watches from a distance while others do not perceive, a child-protection scene built from sustained, unobtrusive sight.
Returning Moses to his mother so her eye is comforted reverses the section's image of a child left without the gaze that keeps him present.
The brothers actually place Joseph in the hidden well, completing 12:9-10's plan to gain attention by removing a child from sight.
Abraham sees a star and then rejects it when it sets; the link is limited to a visible celestial object disappearing, but it cautions against attaching ultimate worth to what captures sight.
